name: Triangle Law
description: A geometric rule for adding two vectors—the head-to-tail method forms a triangle

content.overview: Remember the head-to-tail trick from vector addition? The Triangle Law is just that idea with an official name and a shape to picture: two vectors as two sides, and the sum closes the triangle. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Nothing new to learn here, honestly—the Triangle Law is just a fancier name for the head-to-tail method you might already know. Let's make it concrete: {{viz:diagram-02}}

**Step 1:** Draw vector A starting from the origin
**Step 2:** Draw vector B starting right at the HEAD (the tip) of A
**Step 3:** Draw one last line straight from the origin to B's head—that closing line is A + B.

Boom, you've drawn a triangle! {{viz:anim-01}}

**Example: Two Boats**

Boat 1 zips 5 km east. Boat 2 starts from where Boat 1 ended up and goes 3 km north. So where's Boat 2 relative to the very first starting point?

Draw 5 km east, then from there, 3 km north. The straight-line path back to the start—that's your resultant. Its length works out to √(5² + 3²) = √34 ≈ 5.8 km, sitting at some angle from east.

**The Math Behind It:** {{viz:chart-01}}

Whenever two vectors act as two sides of a triangle, the third side—both its length and direction—gives you their sum. Simple as that.

**Why call it a "Triangle"?**

Because three vectors can form a closed loop: A, B, and the reverse of their sum, -(A+B), snap together into a closed triangle. That's actually a neat trick for checking whether a set of forces balances out to zero.
keyPoints: Triangle Law is just head-to-tail vector addition, dressed up with a name
Two vectors form two sides of the triangle, their sum is the third side
Three vectors can close up into a triangle—great for checking balance
Perfect for finding the resultant of two forces or two displacements
It's a purely graphical method—you don't even need to touch components
content.whyItMatters: This is the picture-in-your-head way to understand vector addition, no formulas required. A ton of physics problems involving forces or displacements get way easier once you can just sketch the triangle and see the answer.
